## The Plumber Who Saw the Leaks: Reading a Brand for Holes Nobody Else Noticed

A man looks at someone else's business the way a plumber looks at a house. Most visitors see a nice kitchen. The plumber hears the drip behind the wall, spots the slow drain, clocks the pipe that's one winter from bursting. Jack Moses did this to a famous podcaster's brand. He wasn't asked to. There was no job opening. He just looked — and where everyone else saw a successful creator, he saw a list of leaks: no Twitter posting, no email capture, no cross-posting of podcast clips, no LinkedIn. Then he did the thing that turns a diagnosis into a paycheck. He walked up to the house and said, "I can fix all of that," and got hired into a role that did not exist five minutes earlier.[^1]

That's the move. You don't apply for a position. You manufacture one out of a gap that only a wide enough skill set lets you see.

## What This Actually Is

Creating a position out of thin air means spotting an unmet need inside someone else's operation, naming it, and proposing yourself as the person who fills it — before anyone has decided the need is worth a hire. The need was always there. What was missing was someone with enough range to see it as an opportunity rather than as noise.[^2]

The engine underneath it is breadth. A specialist who only does one thing sees the world through that one thing's keyhole. A generalist who has stacked several skills sees the whole machine, including the parts that are missing. Moses is explicit that this is downstream of having a broad skill set: "Freelancer B because he has a broader skill set, he can spot opportunities that freelancer A can't."[^3] The position you invent is the visible output of perception nobody else has.

## How the Eye Gets Wide Enough to See the Gap

Vision scales with what you've done with your hands. When Moses was only a ghostwriter — "I needed to be told what to do and I just wrote for people's social media accounts" — he couldn't see opportunities, because his eye was trained on a single task.[^4] As he built his own products and brand and stacked more skills, his field of view widened. Suddenly he could look at a podcaster's whole funnel and see the missing email capture, the absent cross-posting, the unused LinkedIn — because he now understood all of those systems from the inside.[^5]

There are two mechanisms braided together here. The first is plain competence: you can only spot a broken funnel if you know what a working funnel looks like. The second is what Moses calls the internal game — "raising your consciousness and seeing things that you can't previously see."[^6] Strip the metaphysical framing and a defensible operator claim remains: your perception is bounded by your experience, and widening the experience widens the perception. The skills are the lenses. Add a lens and a whole category of opportunity that was invisible snaps into focus.

The delivery mechanism is the network. Moses didn't have a contact line to the podcaster. He routed his proposal "through a connection" up a chain of command until it reached the man, who liked it and hired him.[^7] Seeing the gap is necessary but not sufficient — the proposal still has to travel. Perception plus a path equals a job that didn't exist.

## What This Hands the Rest of the Vault

This page supplies the vault's clearest worked example of skill-stacking converting into raw opportunity. Other pages argue that range is valuable; this one shows range producing a *specific* outcome — a hire — through a *specific* mechanism: seeing holes a narrow operator can't see. It gives the abstract "each skill doubles your odds" claim a concrete causal story.

It also reframes job-getting itself. Most of the vault's career thinking assumes you respond to demand that already exists. This concept says the sharpest operators *generate* demand by making a latent need legible to the person who has it. That's a different posture, and it threads into the vault's positioning and personal-monopoly material as a tactical sibling.

## Analytical Case Study: The Aubrey Marcus Job That Wasn't a Job

Watch the sequence, because the order of operations is the lesson.

Moses starts by choosing the target on alignment, not on whether they're hiring: "Who do I want to work with? I want to work with somebody who is aligned with my values and on a similar path to myself."[^8] He lands on Aubrey Marcus, a big spiritual podcaster. He does not check for an open role. He audits the brand: "He wasn't posting on Twitter. He didn't have a good email capture. He didn't have a good email marketing strategy. He wasn't cross-posting his podcast clips anywhere. He wasn't utilizing Twitter threads... He wasn't on LinkedIn."[^9]

Notice that every hole is a skill Moses already owns. The audit is only possible because his arsenal is wide enough to recognize each absence. A pure copywriter would have seen "a successful podcaster" and moved on. Moses sees a punch list.

Then the proposal: "I saw all these holes and I said, 'I can plug in and do this for them.' And so there wasn't even a job position open, but through a connection that I had... I proposed this idea through a chain of command and it reached him and he really liked it and I got hired."[^10] No application. No waiting for a posting. He named the gap, named himself as the fix, and used a relationship to deliver the message.

The coda is the honest part: about a month in, he realized he didn't want the job at all — he wanted to do his own thing. But he keeps the lesson: "I believe I went through that to learn the skill of you can create your own position out of thin air if you have enough skills and you can see things sufficiently."[^11] The job was disposable. The capability was the prize.

## Implementation Workflow: Auditing a Brand Like a Building Inspector

You're scrolling someone's profile. Not a stranger — someone whose work you actually respect, someone building in a direction you'd be proud to be near. Stop treating it as a fan. Start treating it as an inspector with a clipboard.

You open their Twitter and there's nothing for three weeks. Note it. You go to their site and look for the email signup — it's buried below the fold, or it isn't there. Note it. You watch a podcast clip and check whether it's been cut into shorts anywhere. It hasn't. Note it. Each absence lands in your gut as a small click of recognition: *I could do that. I could do that. I could do that.* The list writes itself, and it's a list of things you already know how to build.

Now you stop and ask who you know. Not a cold DM into the void — a real connection, one human between you and them, or two. You write the proposal as a plan, not a pitch for employment: here are the leaks, here's what fixing them looks like, here's me offering to do it. You hand it to your connection and let it travel up the chain. Then you wait, knowing the worst case is silence and the best case is a position that existed nowhere until your eye conjured it.

## The Invisible-Gap Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

You waited for the posting. You refreshed the careers page instead of auditing the brand — which means you've outsourced your opportunity to whether someone else has already named the need. The whole edge is naming it first.

You see a polished brand and assume it's complete. The drip is behind the wall. If you only see the nice kitchen, your skill set is too narrow to spot the plumbing, and the fix is more range, not more confidence.

You spotted the gap but had no path to the person. The proposal died in your drafts because you never built the connection that carries it. Perception without a relay is a private hunch.

You named yourself the fix for a hole you can't actually patch. This collapses on contact — you get the role and can't deliver, and the reputation cost outlasts the gig.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The core claim is credible operator experience: a wide skill set lets you perceive opportunities a specialist misses.[^12] It's a single first-person anecdote, though — `🚩 SINGLE SOURCE` — and survivorship is doing quiet work. Moses tells the story where the gap-spotting led to a hire; the proposals that went nowhere don't make the highlight reel.

A genuine tension sits at the center: Moses took the manufactured job and quit it inside a month.[^13] Read one way, that confirms the lesson was the *capability*, not the role. Read another way, it's a caution — manufacturing a position you don't actually want burns a relationship and a month for a skill you could have practiced on a target you'd stay with. The transcript leaves this unresolved, and it should stay unresolved here.

The "raising your consciousness" framing of expanded perception is `[POPULAR SOURCE]` and overstates a real thing. The defensible version — experience widens what you can notice — needs no metaphysics. Open question: is gap-spotting trainable directly, or only as a byproduct of stacking skills across years?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Moses and Justin Welsh (and the Perell positioning canon) converge on a shared premise: the market does not come pre-sliced with your name on a slot. Where Perell argues you must *create*, not find, a niche, Moses runs the same logic one level down — into employment itself. Perell says don't look for an empty niche; invent one. Moses says don't look for an empty job; invent one. The structural move is identical: refuse the posture of a searcher, adopt the posture of a maker.

The split shows up in *who supplies the gap*. Perell's creator manufactures a niche out of their own combination of obsessions — the gap is internal, defined by the unrepeatable intersection of what only you care about. Moses's operator finds the gap inside *someone else's* operation — the hole is external, sitting in another person's funnel, waiting to be named. One invents demand from the self; the other harvests latent demand from a target. That difference is the whole reason this page lives in business rather than creative-practice: it's about reading an operation, not expressing a self.

Hormozi would press on the survivorship. His volume-negates-luck stance reframes Moses's one clean Aubrey Marcus story as a single successful draw, and would ask how many audits produced no hire before this one landed. Moses tells it as perception; Hormozi would tell it as reps. The honest synthesis is both: you need the eye *and* enough attempts that the eye gets a chance to pay off. What the disagreement exposes is that "I saw the gap" and "I sent enough proposals that one connected" are two different explanations for the same outcome, and the transcript only gives us the flattering one.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Here's the plain version first: spotting a gap nobody else can see is the same trick whether you're reading a business, a market, or your own creative voice — the wider your range, the more invisible openings light up.

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/each-skill-doubles-odds-of-success|Each Skill Doubles Your Odds of Success]] — This is the parent mechanism, and the handshake is causal rather than thematic. That page argues breadth raises your value and your odds; this page shows *the channel* through which it does — perception. Stack a skill and you don't just become more useful in the abstract; you literally see opportunities that were invisible before, because each skill is a lens trained on a different kind of gap. The Aubrey Marcus audit is impossible for a one-skill freelancer not because they lack confidence but because they lack the lenses. The insight that surfaces only when you read the two together: skill-stacking's real payoff isn't capability, it's *vision* — the capabilities are almost a side effect of the wider field of view they grant.

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/perell-create-not-find-a-niche|Perell — Create Not Find a Niche]] — Both refuse the searcher's posture and adopt the maker's. Perell builds a niche where none existed; Moses builds a job where none existed. Putting them side by side reveals a single underlying law operating at two scales: positions of all kinds — market slots, employment, identity — are not found objects but manufactured ones, and the constraint on manufacturing them is perception, not permission. Reading Perell alone, you'd think niche-creation is a content strategy. Reading Moses alongside it, you see it's a general-purpose operating stance: the world doesn't hand you a labeled slot, so you carve one, and the carving tool is a wide enough eye to see where a slot *should* be. Neither framing, on its own, shows you that "create a niche" and "create a job" are the same gesture pointed at different targets — that only appears when the two pages sit together.

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/luck-surface-area|Luck Surface Area]] — The connection here is the delivery problem. Moses's audit is worthless without the connection that carries his proposal up the chain. Luck surface area explains *why he had a connection to use*: years of action and friendship had built the relay before he needed it. Spotting the gap is the action-luck and opportunity-luck quadrants firing at once; the network is what converts a private observation into a hire. What the pairing makes plain is that gap-spotting and luck-building are not two skills but one loop — the network feeds you the targets to audit, and the audit gives the network something concrete to relay.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication:** If positions are manufactured rather than found, then "there are no jobs in my field" is a confession about your perception, not a fact about the market. Every operation you respect has leaks. The reason you can't see them isn't that they're hidden — it's that your skill set hasn't given you the lenses yet. Unemployment, on this reading, is partly a vision problem dressed up as an economic one.

**Generative Questions:**
- How many gap-audits should an operator run before concluding the eye isn't trained yet versus concluding the proposals aren't traveling? Where's the line between a perception failure and a network failure?
- If manufactured positions are disposable to the manufacturer (Moses quit in a month), what does that do to the *other* party — and is gap-spotting ethical when you already suspect you won't stay?
- Could the entire skill be compressed into a single repeatable audit checklist, or does it die the moment it's proceduralized, because the whole point is seeing what a checklist would miss?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/each-skill-doubles-odds-of-success|Each Skill Doubles Your Odds of Success]] — the parent principle; breadth is what makes the gaps visible in the first place.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/luck-surface-area|Luck Surface Area]] — supplies the connection that delivers the proposal; gap-spotting is one of its luck quadrants in action.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/freelance-without-becoming-the-skill|Freelance Without Becoming the Skill]] — the same wide-range posture, applied to keeping your identity unboxed rather than to inventing a role.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/perell-create-not-find-a-niche|Perell — Create Not Find a Niche]] — the same manufacture-don't-search move at the level of market positioning.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/butcher-personal-monopoly-3c-framework|Butcher 3C Framework]] — the personal-monopoly version: your unrepeatable combination is itself a position carved from nothing.

title: Cringe Maxing Perfectionism Antidote

## Ten Minutes to Press Post: Cringe as the Toll Booth

The first tweet Jack Moses ever tried to send nearly didn't go out. His body was freaking out — anxious, sweating, cringing at a screen no one else had seen yet. It took him ten minutes to press post. When he finally did, his whole body spasmed and he threw his phone across the room.[^1] Nothing about the tweet mattered. The whole drama was internal — a nervous system convinced that publishing one sentence was a threat to survival.

That moment, Moses says, is exactly what most people are avoiding. Not bad writing, not failure — the raw discomfort of stepping past the known edge of who you think you are.[^2] His answer is a deliberately ugly word: cringe maxing. Stop trying to feel comfortable. Go toward the cringe on purpose, max it out, and let it burn off.

## What This Actually Is

Cringe maxing is the antidote to perfectionism, and it works by detaching your self-worth from your output.[^3] The perfectionist can't publish because every post feels like a verdict on their whole self. Cringe maxing breaks that wire: you take an action, it sucks, you take another one, maybe everyone's laughing at you in your head — and then you just get better.[^4] The cringe doesn't disappear because you got good. It disappears because you stopped needing it not to be there.

The deeper claim is that this is a *spiritual* act, not a marketing tactic. What looks like a person posting content is actually a person doing internal work to transcend the need for other people's validation — creating from their own heart and intrinsic motivation instead of from the crowd's approval.[^5] Pushing through cringe is how you train that muscle in public.

## The Toll Booth: Why the Discomfort Is the Mechanism

Picture cringe as a toll booth between the self you are and the self you're trying to become. Moses's framing is that the post is going to make you cringe, and you know it — but if you put it out, it leads you onto a higher trajectory than the one you're on.[^6] The toll isn't a side effect of the journey. It *is* the journey. Every time you pay it, you cross a little further past the boundary of the old identity.

The body is what collects the toll. Moses describes letting the old self and the body-mind "do its thing and run its course" while the higher self knows it's taking the right action.[^7] The spasm, the sweat, the urge to delete — that's stored insecurity processing itself out through the nervous system. Try to skip the discomfort and you never cross; the perfectionist stays parked at the booth forever, polishing a draft, mistaking endless preparation for progress.[^8] Cringe maxing is just the decision to pay the toll repeatedly until the road past it becomes familiar and the booth stops feeling like a wall.

## What This Gives the Rest of the Vault

This page is the emotional engine behind every "just publish" principle in the cluster. The vault's pages on iteration, on getting in the arena, on volume — all of them assume you can actually hit post. This one names the precise internal obstacle that stops people from doing so and supplies the reframe that gets them through it. It converts "ship more" from a directive into a felt practice: it tells you what the resistance *is* (identity defending itself) and why walking into it is the work, not a detour from it.

## Analytical Case Study: Throwing the Phone Across the Room

Replay the scene in slow motion, because every beat is diagnostic. Moses is twenty-something, untrained in body awareness, about to publish his first tweet. The anxiety isn't proportional to the stakes — one tweet from an account nobody follows cannot meaningfully harm him. Yet his body responds as if to genuine danger: sweat, racing pulse, ten full minutes of paralysis with his thumb over the button.[^9]

The tell is the phone flying across the room *after* he posts. The threat was never the audience's reaction — he hadn't gotten one yet. The threat was the act of exposure itself, the crossing past "the known confines of the ego and of the personal identity."[^10] His nervous system was defending a self-image, and publishing breached it. Now run the same person forward: today he posts a tweet and doesn't think about it.[^11] The cringe didn't get argued away. It got *metabolized* — paid down, post by post, until the identity expanded to include "person who publishes." The thrown phone is the purest evidence that cringe is an inside job, with the outside world barely involved.

## Implementation Workflow: The Story You Know Your High School Friends Will See

You're about to put something on your Instagram story — a clip of you talking about ideas your old high school friends would find ridiculous. Your thumb stops. You can feel them watching: *these people are all going to see me talk about this crazy stuff.* The cringe rises right on cue.[^12]

Don't wait for it to pass. Name it instead — *yes, this is going to make me cringe, and the people from my old life will think it's weird.* Let that be true. Then notice the second, quieter fact underneath: the cringe is information that you're crossing the boundary, not a signal to stop. Hold both at once.

Now post it without resolving the feeling. Watch what your body does — maybe a flush of heat, maybe the impulse to delete it in an hour. Let the impulse exist and don't obey it. You're not performing for the high school friends; you're practicing creating from your own heart while their imagined judgment sits in the room with you. After enough reps, the thing Moses promises arrives: you simply stop caring. And that not-caring is the freedom — the point where you can finally give your fullest gift to the world.[^13]

## The Perfectionism Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

You can recognize the perfectionist trap by its symptoms. The work never ships because it's never good enough — every draft is one more revision away from being safe to expose.[^14] Self-worth is fused to the output, so a flat post doesn't feel like a flat post, it feels like proof you're not good enough. There's endless "solution searching" and preparation — courses, plans, research — all of it a sophisticated way to stay parked at the toll booth without admitting it.[^15]

The deepest sign is that the person is governed by an audience that isn't even paying attention. They imagine everyone laughing, when, as Moses bluntly notes, no one actually cares.[^16] The perfectionist has outsourced their nervous system to a crowd of phantom critics. The cure isn't better work. It's the willingness to cringe in front of the phantoms until they lose their grip.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The core practice is credible operator experience — the first-post terror and its gradual extinction through repetition is a textbook exposure-and-habituation arc, recognizable to anyone who has built a public presence.[^17] [PARAPHRASED] "No one actually cares" is a defensible practitioner read on the spotlight effect.

Two flags belong here. First, the man-in-the-arena quote: Moses and Will attribute it to "Timothy Roosevelt," hedging with "I'm probably butchering that."[^18] [UNVERIFIED] The actual line is from Theodore Roosevelt's 1910 "Citizenship in a Republic" speech; the misattribution is acknowledged in the transcript but should not be repeated as fact. Second, the framing of posting as a "spiritual action" and the language of "higher self," "higher timeline," and raising consciousness sit inside the hosts' broader metaphysical worldview.[^19] [POPULAR SOURCE] 🚩 MOTIVATED REASONING — the hosts sell community and retreats built on this spiritual-growth framing, so the spiritualization of routine exposure therapy should be read as Moses's interpretation, not as an established mechanism. Stripped of the metaphysics, the practical claim — detach self-worth from output, ship anyway, habituate — stands on its own.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Moses and David Butcher are describing the same act from two altitudes. Butcher's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/butcher-iterators-beat-perfectionists-non-monotonic-growth|iterators beat perfectionists]] thesis is structural and external: progress is non-monotonic, the iterator who ships ugly and often outperforms the perfectionist who waits, because volume and feedback compound while polishing in private does not. Moses agrees completely on the conclusion — take an action, it sucks, take another, get better — but he's looking *inside* the iterator at the moment of shipping.[^20] Where Butcher describes the curve, Moses describes the cringe that the curve costs you to walk.

The convergence is total at the level of advice; the divergence is in what each man thinks the real obstacle is. For Butcher the obstacle is a flawed mental model of how growth works — fix the model and you'll iterate. For Moses the obstacle is somatic and identity-deep — your body will fight you even after you intellectually accept that iteration wins. That split is the useful part. It explains why people who *fully understand* that iterators win still can't press post: knowing the curve doesn't pay the toll. Butcher gives you the reason to ship; Moses gives you the method for surviving the feeling of shipping. The first is necessary and not sufficient; the second is what carries you across when the first runs out.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Put simply: this page says the thing blocking you from publishing isn't bad work, it's the feeling of exposure — and that connects both to how creative growth actually compounds and to old contemplative practices of acting past the ego.

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/butcher-iterators-beat-perfectionists-non-monotonic-growth|Iterators Beat Perfectionists]].** Butcher proves *why* you should ship ugly; Moses handles *what it feels like* to do it. The structural parallel is that both reject the perfectionist's premise that the next draft will finally be safe — Butcher because the data says iteration wins, Moses because the safety the perfectionist is chasing is an internal state no draft can deliver. The tension that makes them worth reading together is that Butcher's argument is rational and Moses's obstacle is irrational: you can be fully persuaded by the iteration curve and still throw your phone across the room. What surfaces from holding the two together is a gap that neither closes alone — the distance between *understanding* that iterators win and *being able* to iterate. That gap is pure cringe, and it explains the most common failure in creative work: people who have read all the right advice, agree with all of it, and still don't post. The model change is necessary; the toll still has to be paid by a body.

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/arts-and-music-as-sadhana|Arts and Music as Sadhana]].** Moses calls cringe maxing a spiritual journey — transcending the need for others' validation, creating from your own intrinsic spirit.[^21] Sadhana is the contemplative discipline of repeated daily practice aimed at loosening the ego's grip. The parallel is exact at the level of structure: both are reps performed against internal resistance, where the resistance *is* the material being worked, and both promise that what feels unbearable at first becomes effortless through repetition — Moses posts without a thought now; the practitioner's once-difficult practice becomes second nature. The insight the link draws out, which the marketing frame would miss: cringe maxing is exposure therapy and ego-dissolution wearing the same clothes. The discomfort of publishing and the discomfort of sitting through a hard practice are the same boundary being crossed — the edge of the defended self — which is why Moses can plausibly call hitting "post" a spiritual act without entirely stretching the word. The difference worth keeping is that sadhana usually crosses that edge in private, while cringe maxing crosses it in front of an audience, which adds a layer the contemplative frame doesn't account for: the witness. Posting isn't only the ego meeting its own resistance; it's the ego meeting its resistance *with everyone watching* — which makes it harder, and arguably makes the habituation stick faster, because there's no private retreat to hide the practice in.

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/conviction-corrects-tone-trick-vs-train|Conviction Corrects Tone (Hormozi)]].** Hormozi's principle is that genuine belief in what you're saying fixes the tone of how you say it — the manipulative edge drains out when you're convinced you're helping. Cringe maxing is the same move pointed inward: creating from your own heart and intrinsic motivation rather than the crowd's approval. The structural parallel is that both locate the cure for a surface problem (bad tone, blocked publishing) in an internal shift (conviction, detached self-worth) rather than in technique. The tension that makes them productive together is the direction of the gaze. Hormozi's conviction is about your relationship to the *message* — do you believe it? Moses's detachment is about your relationship to the *audience* — do you need them to approve? What falls out once you hold both, and neither names alone: the creator who has both conviction in the message and indifference to the verdict is unstoppable, because there's nothing left to manipulate *and* nothing left to fear. The perfectionist usually lacks the second; the manipulator usually lacks the first. Cringe maxing trains the indifference; conviction supplies the belief; you need the pair to create freely.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication.** The destabilizing reading is that your standards might be a disguise for your fear. The perfectionist tells a flattering story — *I just have high standards, I care about quality* — but the cringe scene suggests the standards are often a respectable cover for a nervous system that doesn't want to be seen. If that's true, then "I'll post it when it's good enough" isn't discernment at all. It's the toll booth, dressed up as taste.

**Generative Questions.**
- How do you tell genuine quality control apart from fear wearing the mask of high standards — is there any test from the inside, or only the willingness to ship and find out?
- If habituation eventually kills the cringe entirely, do you lose something — is a little residual cringe the signal that you're still crossing a real edge rather than coasting?
- Moses frames posting as transcending others' opinions, yet the creator economy runs on others' attention. Can you truly stop caring what people think while still building a business on what they click?

## Connected Concepts
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/butcher-iterators-beat-perfectionists-non-monotonic-growth|Iterators Beat Perfectionists]] — the structural case for shipping ugly; this page supplies the internal method for actually doing it.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/one-to-three-degrees-of-separation|One to Three Degrees of Separation]] — the pedestal that blocks the cold email is the same exposure fear that blocks the first post.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/arts-and-music-as-sadhana|Arts and Music as Sadhana]] — repeated practice against internal resistance; the contemplative twin of cringe maxing.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/conviction-corrects-tone-trick-vs-train|Conviction Corrects Tone (Hormozi)]] — creating from your own conviction rather than the crowd's approval, the positive form of transcending validation.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/perell-irrationally-passionate-patient-10-year-horizon|Irrationally Passionate and Patient — 10-Year Horizon]] — the long game that only begins once you can survive publishing at all.

# Curiosity Is the Registration Page

## The Photo You Can't Stop Staring At

You land on a webinar sign-up page and there's a picture of the host doing something that makes no sense — holding an object, in a pose, with no obvious connection to anything. You have no idea what it means. And you can't quite look away.

That confusion is the whole design. Brunson's rule for a high-converting registration page is a single word: "CURIOSITY. That's it."[^1]

His diagnosis of a page that *doesn't* convert is just as blunt. "If your registration page isn't converting well, it's because you're showing people too much and they assume they know the answer."[^2] The moment a visitor thinks they know what the webinar is about, they leave — because knowing removes the reason to register.

So the registration page isn't trying to inform. It's trying to open a question the visitor can only close by signing up. The strange photo, the teasing headline — every element exists to make the visitor need to know, and to make registration the only way to find out.

Everything you'd normally put on a "good" web page works against you here. Clarity, completeness, a helpful explainer video, a tidy bullet list of what you'll learn — all of it answers questions, and answered questions are exits. The registration page is the one page in your business where being informative is a liability.

## Curiosity Is the Whole Game

Flip the usual logic of a landing page. Most pages try to *convince* — here's what you'll learn, here's the value, here are the bullet points. Brunson says that's exactly backwards for a webinar.[^3]

"If they think they know what you're going to talk about, then they won't register or show up. If they can't figure out what it is without registering, then you'll get them to register AND show up."[^4]

The insight is that registration is powered by an *unanswered* question, not a satisfied one. A page that fully explains the webinar has given the visitor the payoff for free — there's nothing left to get by signing up. A page that opens a compelling gap and refuses to close it makes registration the only path to relief.

This is why "showing too much" kills conversion. Every additional detail is a piece of the question answered, and an answered question is a reason not to register. The page has to say *enough* to make the visitor want the answer and *not enough* for them to guess it.

It's the movie-trailer problem in reverse. A bad trailer shows you the whole plot, and now you don't need the film. A good one shows you a world and a question and sends you to the theater to resolve it. The registration page is a trailer whose only job is to make you buy the ticket.

## The Nonsensical Image, and Why Video Loses

The strange photo does specific work. "The picture makes NO sense. When you look at it, you have no idea what it is or why I'm doing it. It arouses curiosity."[^5] Brunson's guidance: find a picture of yourself "kinda related to the topic but kinda strange."[^6]

A clear, explanatory image would tell the visitor what the webinar is about — and telling them is the mistake. A strange one does the opposite: it poses a visual question. *Why is he doing that?* The only image that helps is one that refuses to explain itself.

This is also why he recommends against video on the registration page. "Rarely (if ever) will it beat a strange image."[^7] A video, by its nature, explains — it shows, tells, demonstrates. It answers questions the page is trying to keep open. The strange still image withholds; the video reveals. And on a page whose only job is to make you need to register, revealing is defeat.

The counterintuitive lesson: the more your page communicates, the worse it converts, because communication closes the gap that registration was supposed to close.

## The Unanswered-Question Headline

The headline is where curiosity is engineered most deliberately. Brunson's example: "My Weird Niche Funnel That's Currently Making Me $17,947 Per Day...And How You Can ETHICALLY Knock It Off In Less Than 10 Minutes!"[^8]

Look at how much it refuses to tell you. What niche? Is $17,947 a day really possible? Can you *ethically* knock it off — how? In ten minutes? Brunson lists these open loops himself: the headline "gives you a hint about the presentation, but it leaves SO many unanswered questions."[^9]

Every one of those questions is a hook. The headline is built as a cluster of gaps, each one a thing you'd have to register to resolve. The oddly specific number ($17,947, not "about $18k") adds credibility-through-precision while deepening the mystery — a made-up round number invites doubt, but a strange exact one invites "wait, is that real?"

The formula underneath is the opportunity-switch headline — "how to [result] without [fear]" — loaded with enough specificity to be tantalizing and enough withholding to stay a question. The whole line is a locked door with a very interesting shape.

## Analytical Case Study: The Too-Much-Information Failure

The failure mode is worth examining because it's the opposite of what intuition suggests.[^10]

A well-meaning expert builds a registration page and does what feels responsible: explains the webinar clearly. Here's the topic, here's what we'll cover, here are the five things you'll learn, here's a video of me walking you through it. It's honest, thorough, professional. And it converts terribly.

Why? Because every clear sentence answered a question, and every answered question removed a reason to register. By the end of the page, the visitor thinks *"I get it — it's a webinar about X, teaching Y."* And thinking they get it, they leave. Not because they weren't interested, but because the page satisfied the interest instead of stoking it.

The strange thing this reveals: on a registration page, clarity is a conversion killer and confusion is a conversion driver — within limits. The visitor has to be confused in the specific way that makes them want the answer (a compelling gap), not the way that makes them bounce (a page that makes no sense at all). Brunson's "kinda related but kinda strange" is the exact calibration: related enough to signal relevance, strange enough to withhold the payoff. The failure isn't too little information or too much — it's information that closes the gap instead of opening it.

## Where Curiosity Tips into Clickbait

The honest core is real. A registration page genuinely can't give away the whole webinar, and an open question is a legitimate reason to attend — you sign up because you want to know, and then you find out. That's a fair trade.

The manipulation is when the gap is a lie. Curiosity converts to clickbait the moment the headline promises an answer the webinar doesn't deliver — when "$17,947 a day, ethically knocked off in 10 minutes" opens a gap that the presentation never honestly closes. The technique is neutral; the question is whether the answer behind the door is worth the door.

The specific edge here is the precision-as-credibility move. "$17,947 per day" reads as real *because* it's oddly exact, but the exactness is a persuasion device, not evidence — a round number invites skepticism, a strange precise one borrows the texture of truth without earning it. A curiosity gap built on a fabricated-but-precise number is manipulative in a way a gap built on a real one isn't, and the visitor can't tell them apart from the page. The honest version opens a gap it can actually close; the manipulative one opens a gap around a promise it can't keep, dressed in a number specific enough to feel true.

## Implementation Workflow

You're building a registration page. Your instinct is to explain the webinar clearly. Fight it.

You pick an image of yourself that's "kinda related but kinda strange" — one that poses a visual question instead of answering one. You skip the video, because video explains and explaining is losing. You write a headline that's a cluster of open loops: a specific, tantalizing hint that leaves several sharp questions unanswered.

You test your page against one question: after reading it, does the visitor think they know what the webinar is about? If yes, you've shown too much — cut detail until they're curious instead of satisfied.

Then the honesty gate. A curiosity gap is fair when the webinar actually closes it — when the answer behind the door is worth the door. It tips into clickbait when the headline opens a gap the presentation can't honestly resolve, or leans on a precise-but-fabricated number to borrow credibility it didn't earn. Open questions you can truthfully answer. If your best hook requires a promise you can't keep, the page will convert and the webinar will disappoint — and the model that depends on repeat traffic can't afford a reputation for locked doors with nothing behind them.

## Diagnostic: Opening a Gap or Baiting a Click?

**Opening a gap** poses a genuine question the visitor wants answered and the webinar honestly resolves — the door is interesting and the room behind it delivers.

**Baiting a click** opens a gap around a promise the presentation can't keep, or dresses a fabricated claim in precise numbers to feel true — the door is interesting and the room is empty.

The test is whether the webinar closes the gap the page opened. If the headline's questions get real answers in the presentation, the curiosity was honest. If the visitor registers to learn "how you ethically knock off a $17,947-a-day funnel in 10 minutes" and the webinar never delivers that, the page baited the click — and precise numbers on the promise make the bait more effective, not more honest.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

The page rests on Brunson's own registration-page doctrine and curiosity-gap psychology that's well-documented but uncited.[^11] The $17,947 headline is a worked example, not a verified figure.

**Tension:** an open question is a legitimate reason to register, and a gap around an undeliverable promise is clickbait, and the same technique produces both — the visitor can't tell an honest gap from a manipulative one from the page alone.

**Second tension:** precision reads as credibility ("$17,947" feels truer than "$18k"), but the precision is a persuasion device, not evidence. A fabricated-but-exact number weaponizes the visitor's instinct that specificity means truth.

**Open question:** if clarity kills conversion and confusion drives it, is there a stable line between an honest curiosity gap and clickbait — or does the mechanism that makes registration pages work (withhold the payoff) inherently reward promising more than you deliver, since the gap converts whether or not the answer is worth it?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Convergence with the-five-curiosity-hooks and the-opportunity-switch-headline pages is direct — the registration page is where those tools land first. The opportunity-switch headline ("how to [result] without [fear]") is the page's headline formula, and the five curiosity hooks are the positioning that fills the gap the page opens.

The tension with Brunson's own "give value" ethos is quiet but present. The webinar model runs on giving away real teaching to build trust — yet the registration page is engineered to *withhold*, to convert through what it refuses to say. The generosity starts after the sign-up; the page itself is pure withholding. The book doesn't mark the switch from "give everything" (the webinar) to "reveal nothing" (the page that gets them there), but the two live one click apart.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/information-gap-curiosity|Information-Gap Curiosity]].** Curiosity fires when we become aware of a gap between what we know and what we want to know — and the discomfort of the open gap drives us to close it. The registration page manufactures that gap deliberately and offers registration as the only way to close it.

Here is what neither page catches on its own: **the page's power isn't that it interests you — it's that it makes you *aware of a specific thing you don't know*, which is a different and stronger force, because an unanswered question is an itch and registration is the only scratch.** The information-gap page explains why known-unknowns compel us. This page shows the specific engineering: "showing too much" fails because it closes gaps, and the whole design is to open a gap of exactly the right size — big enough to itch, not so big it reads as noise. Taken separately, neither shows that the failure mode of a landing page is *answering* — that the responsible instinct to explain clearly is precisely what removes the gap the registration was meant to close. Interest attracts; an open loop compels; the page trades the first for the second.

**To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-wait-what-hook-juxtaposition-orlean|The "Wait, What?" Hook]].** A strong opening line creates a jolt of confusion through juxtaposition — two things that don't belong together, forcing the reader to keep going to resolve the dissonance. The nonsensical registration-page image is the visual version: a photo that doesn't make sense, held open as a question.

What neither says alone, both say together: **the strange image and the "wait, what?" sentence are the same device in different media — deliberate, calibrated confusion that the audience can only resolve by continuing — and both fail identically when they explain too much.** The craft page shows the technique serving comprehension and delight (a great opening line pulls you into a story worth reading). This page shows the identical technique serving conversion (a strange image pulls you into a sign-up). Taken separately, neither shows that the writer's opening hook and the marketer's registration image are governed by the same rule — withhold enough to compel, reveal enough to stay relevant — and that the ethical difference lives entirely in whether what's behind the hook is worth the reader's continued attention. Same mechanism, and the honesty is downstream of it.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** A registration page's job is not to inform but to open a question the visitor can only close by signing up — which is why "showing too much" is the cardinal sin: every clear sentence answers a question, and an answered question removes a reason to register. Curiosity runs on the *unanswered*, so the page uses a strange image (that poses a visual question instead of answering one), skips video (which explains, and explaining is losing), and writes a headline that's a cluster of open loops around a tantalizing, oddly precise number. The failure mode is the opposite of intuition: the responsible, thorough, clearly-explained page converts terribly, because clarity satisfies the interest instead of stoking it, and a satisfied visitor leaves. Confusion — of the specific "kinda related but kinda strange" kind — is the conversion driver. The ethical edge is that the technique is neutral and the honesty is downstream: a curiosity gap is fair when the webinar closes it, and clickbait when the headline opens a gap the presentation can't keep, or dresses a fabricated claim in precise numbers to borrow the texture of truth. The mechanism rewards withholding whether or not the answer is worth it — which is exactly why the discipline has to come from the operator, not the page.

**Generative questions.**

If clarity kills conversion and withholding drives it, is there a stable line between an honest curiosity gap and clickbait — or does the mechanism that makes registration pages work inherently reward promising more than you deliver, since the gap converts regardless of what's behind the door?

Precise numbers read as truer than round ones, which means fabricated exactness ("$17,947") out-converts honest approximation ("about $18k"). Does the fact that specificity persuades independent of accuracy mean the most honest marketers are structurally disadvantaged against the most precise liars?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/the-opportunity-switch-headline|The Opportunity-Switch Headline]] — the "how to X without Y" formula the page's headline uses
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/the-five-curiosity-hooks|The Five Curiosity Hooks]] — the positioning that fills the gap the page opens

# Customer Acquisition Cost Below Zero

## Getting Paid to Find Customers

Every business that advertises has the same ceiling. You spend money to find a customer, and how many customers you can find is capped by how much money you have. Raise more, spend more, grow faster. That's the whole logic of venture funding.

Brunson claims he removed the cap.

Not by spending less. By making the act of finding a customer *profitable in itself* — so the more customers he acquired, the more money he had to acquire more.[^1]

His competitors and the VCs who tried to invest, he says, couldn't work out how his cost to acquire a customer was "better than free."[^1]

## The Arithmetic

It's simple enough to state in three lines.

You spend, say, $20 in ads to find someone. They buy a $47 information product. You are now $27 up, and you have a customer.

Later, you offer that customer the software subscription that was always the real business. Its acquisition cost is zero — already paid, by them.

Normally the sequence is: spend money → get customer → hope they're worth more than you spent. Brunson's is: spend money → get paid → *also* get customer.

The customer funds their own acquisition, plus margin.

## Why This Changes the Shape of a Company

Two consequences follow, and the second is the one that matters.

**Advertising stops being a budget item.** If ads return more than they cost on the first transaction, spending is limited by how much inventory of attention exists, not by your bank balance. Brunson describes acquiring "tens of thousands of customers, almost overnight, without spending any money out of our pockets."[^1]

**You don't need outside money.** This is the part he's actually arguing. ClickFunnels grew without venture capital, and the negative-CAC mechanism is his explanation for how. It's also why the anti-VC hostility runs through the whole book — the manifesto, the "us vs. them" script, the Funnel Hacker identity are all built against venture-backed competitors.[^2]

The financial mechanism and the tribal identity are the same fact wearing two hats.

## Analytical Case Study: Where It Would Fail Invisibly

The claim is unaudited, so the useful work is asking where a model like this breaks without anyone noticing.

**Churn.** If the information buyers convert to subscribers who cancel at month three, the acquisition wasn't free — it was deferred. Lifetime value, not first-transaction margin, is what determines whether the model holds, and Brunson gives no churn figure anywhere.[^3]

**Buyer mismatch.** The people who buy a $47 book about funnels are not necessarily the people who will pay monthly for funnel software. A front end that converts brilliantly can select for exactly the wrong customer — the perpetual learner who buys information and never implements. This failure looks like success for months.

**Ad-cost drift.** The arithmetic depends on the ad being cheaper than the product. Brunson's own origin story is Google tripling its ad costs and killing his business overnight.[^4] The model that saved him is not structurally immune to the thing that broke him; it just has more margin to absorb it.

None of these are hypothetical objections. They're the standard failure modes of this exact model, and the book addresses none.

## What It Requires That Brunson Underplays

The mechanism needs a front-end product that both sells at a profit *and* makes the back-end product feel necessary. That's a demanding pair of constraints.

Sell something too good and standalone, and the buyer's problem is solved — no reason to continue. Sell something too thin, and it doesn't convert or it burns trust.

The front end has to be genuinely useful and genuinely incomplete. That's a narrow target, and hitting it is most of the work the arithmetic makes look easy.

## Implementation Workflow

You already sell something with a real margin, and you're paying for customers.

Work out what a customer costs you right now. Total ad spend last quarter, divided by customers acquired. One number.

Now think about what you explain to those customers before they buy — the argument, not the pitch. The thing you'd say to a stranger to make your product make sense.

Ask whether someone would pay a small amount for that argument on its own. Not the product. The argument.

If the answer is plainly no, this model isn't available to you and you should stop here rather than forcing it.

If the answer is maybe, price it below what a customer currently costs you and see what happens. You're not testing whether it's profitable yet. You're testing whether the people who buy it are the same people who buy the real thing — and you find that out by tracking the two purchases against each other, which most operators never bother to instrument.

## Diagnostic: Does Your Business Qualify?

Three conditions, all required.

**A back end with recurring or high-margin revenue.** The front end is a loss-leader that happens not to lose; the money is behind it.

**A gap in belief, not information.** The model works where customers don't buy because they don't yet understand why they need it. It doesn't work where they understand perfectly and are choosing a competitor on price.

**A repeatable argument.** If the reason to buy is different for every customer, you can't package it.

Miss any one and you're just selling two things to the same people, which is fine but isn't this.

## The Version That Isn't New

Worth grounding, because the framing is more novel than the mechanism.

Direct-response marketing has run this structure for a century. The loss-leader, the free sample that isn't quite free, the razor sold cheap against blades sold dear — all of them are the same move: subsidize entry, profit on continuation.

What's genuinely different in Brunson's version is two things.

The front end isn't a discounted version of the product. It's a *different category of good* — information about the product, which costs almost nothing to reproduce and therefore carries margin a physical loss-leader can't.

And the front end does persuasive work the razor never did. A cheap razor doesn't explain why you need blades. A book about funnels spends 60,000 words establishing that you need a funnel.

So the information product is simultaneously the loss-leader, the margin, and the sales argument — three jobs in one artifact. That compression is the actual innovation, and it's only available to sellers whose product needs explaining.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

Entirely self-reported, with no accounting, no timeframe, no churn data, and no third-party corroboration.[^3] `[UNVERIFIED]`. The claim is also structurally self-referential: the evidence for the model is the existence of the book making the claim, which is itself the front-end product in the funnel it describes.

**Tension:** Brunson presents negative CAC as a strategy any operator can adopt. But the mechanism requires an audience willing to buy information about your category — which exists in some markets (marketing, fitness, real estate, trading) and barely exists in others. Nobody is buying a $47 course about industrial fasteners. The model is far more domain-bound than the book admits, and the domains where it works overlap almost exactly with the domains where "experts" already sell to each other.

**Open question worth flagging:** in a market where everyone runs this model, the front-end products compete with each other for the same buyers, and the arbitrage closes. Is negative CAC a durable structure or a temporary advantage that ends once the tactic spreads? The book was written in 2017, near the top of that spread.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Set against the vault's existing funnel-metrics material, Brunson's model adds a stage that sits before anything the standard four-metric architecture measures. That corpus tracks what happens once someone enters the funnel; this mechanism is about who enters and who paid for them to.

Against the creator-economy material, the divergence is about sequencing. The audience-first position treats monetization as something you earn the right to later. Brunson monetizes at the first touch, deliberately, because the first-touch revenue is the engine. Neither is obviously right — but they produce very different businesses, and an operator following both at once will be paralysed.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/four-metric-funnel-architecture-show-offer-close-cash-collected|Four-Metric Funnel Architecture]].** That page treats the funnel as a measurement structure with four intervention points. Negative CAC operates entirely upstream of the first one, and that placement is the insight: **the most consequential funnel decision is made before any funnel metric exists.** An operator optimizing show-rate and close-rate is tuning a machine whose economics were fixed by whether the entry was profitable. Held together, the two pages produce a diagnostic the metrics page can't give alone — if your funnel numbers are healthy and the business still can't grow, the constraint isn't in the measured stages at all.

**To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/scarcity-bias|Scarcity Bias]].** Scarcity works by making a resource feel constrained. Negative CAC is the operator's own escape from a real constraint — the acquisition budget — and what's striking is that the same operator then manufactures artificial constraints for the buyer, via deadlines and limited bonuses. **The model removes scarcity from the seller's side of the transaction and installs it on the buyer's.** Neither page states that alone, and it reframes what the deadline is doing: not merely a conversion tactic but the counterpart to an economics in which the seller has no urgency whatsoever, since they can acquire indefinitely. The asymmetry is the product.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The interesting claim isn't that information products are profitable. It's that a business can be structured so growth funds itself at the point of acquisition — which converts capital from a prerequisite into an accelerant, and explains why a category of company could out-grow venture-backed rivals without raising. Whether the specific numbers are real is unverifiable; the structure is what carries forward.

**Generative questions.**

If the model requires a market that buys information about itself, what does that select for at the level of an entire industry? Which sectors are structurally excluded, and does that predict where this style of company never appeared?

Does the mechanism survive its own popularity, or does it close like every arbitrage?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/the-two-types-of-expert-business|The Two Types of Expert Business]] — the model this arithmetic underwrites
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/the-self-liquidating-offer|The Self-Liquidating Offer]] — the same mechanism at the level of a single page
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/the-deliberate-incompleteness|The Deliberate Incompleteness]] — how the front end stays useful and unfinished
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/the-us-versus-them-manifesto-script|The Us-Versus-Them Manifesto Script]] — the anti-VC identity this mechanism licenses
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/four-metric-funnel-architecture-show-offer-close-cash-collected|Four-Metric Funnel Architecture]] — the measured stages this sits upstream of
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/scarcity-bias|Scarcity Bias]] — the constraint removed from one side and installed on the other

[^1]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/brunson-expert-secrets|Brunson, Expert Secrets]] — lines 496–512, the negative-CAC claim and the "better than free" framing. `[UNVERIFIED]`
[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/brunson-expert-secrets|Brunson, Expert Secrets]] — lines 1576–1587 and 1609–1629, the anti-VC manifesto and the Funnel Hacker "us vs. them" script.
[^3]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/brunson-expert-secrets|Brunson, Expert Secrets]] — Limitations: no accounting, timeframe, churn figure, or third-party corroboration for any revenue or acquisition claim. `[UNVERIFIED]`

## The Farmer Who Grows His Own Buyers: Cultivation Over Capture

Picture two people standing at the edge of a wheat field. The first one waits at the gate with a scythe, ready to cut down whatever has already grown tall on its own. The second one is out in the dirt, planting seed, watering, watching a green field come up over a season. The first one is most marketers. They wait for someone who is already hungry, already shopping, already "in the market," and they try to grab them at the gate. Dan Koe does the second thing. He grows the field himself.[^1]

The counterintuitive core is this: you do not have to find customers who already want what you sell. You can make them. You gather a broad audience that has no specific desire yet, and you teach them — slowly, post by post — into the worldview where your product is the obvious next step.[^2] By the time they buy, they were not intercepted. They were cultivated.

## What This Actually Is: Educating Demand Into Existence

Most selling assumes demand is fixed. There is a "starving market" out there, and your job is to locate it, niche down on its problem, and intercept it at the exact moment it reaches for a credit card.[^3] Koe inverts the assumption. Demand is not fixed. It is manufactured upstream, by education, by the people someone surrounds themselves with, and by what they have been conditioned to see as opportunity.[^4]

Strip away Koe's language and the mechanism is plain. People buy when their identity tells them to want a thing. Identity is built by what they learn. So if you control the teaching, you partly control the wanting. The "create customers" move is just getting in early — meeting people while they are still at the bottom of awareness, broad and unsorted, and walking them up the ladder until the product fits.[^5]

## The Internal Logic: Why the Learner Becomes the Buyer

Koe's load-bearing claim is that humans are learning machines.[^6] We are always being educated into some identity, by someone. The question is never whether your prospect is being conditioned — they are, constantly. The question is whether you are the one doing it.

Here is the chain. A person learns a frame. The frame changes who they think they are. Who they think they are changes what they reach for. A standard marketer waits until that whole chain has already run and then tries to catch the output. Koe runs the chain himself. He takes a person who does not yet know they have a problem, makes them feel the problem, shows them a solution exists, and only then names the product as the fast path through.[^7]

Think of it like a river. The interceptor builds a dam at the mouth, downstream, hoping enough water has already collected to be worth catching. Koe goes up to the headwaters and digs the channel that decides where the water flows in the first place. You are not fighting over an existing pool of demand. You are deciding the riverbed.

## What This Gives the Rest of the Vault: The Upstream Move

This page hands the vault a specific upstream principle that other selling and positioning pages can lean on. The [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/nepq-eight-stage-engagement-master-spine|NEPQ Eight-Stage Engagement Master Spine]] is a conversation-level machine — it works on one human, in one call, who has already shown up. Customer creation is the same logic stretched across months and an entire audience: the education sequence is a slow, public version of the engagement spine, run on thousands of strangers before any of them ever talk to you.

It also gives [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/perell-create-not-find-a-niche|Perell — Create, Don't Find a Niche]] its economic engine. Perell argues you build a niche rather than discover one. Koe explains *why that pays*: a created niche is full of people you educated, which means they already trust your frame by the time you sell. And it connects to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/self-persuasion-principle-prospect-persuades-themselves|Self-Persuasion Principle]] — because a customer who learned their way into wanting the thing experiences the purchase as their own conclusion, not your pitch.

## Analytical Case Study: The Marketer at the Gate vs. the Brand at the Bottom

Koe lays out the standard guru playbook and then walks straight through its failures.[^8] The advice: find a starving market, build a product for it, attract that market as your audience. He concedes it works. Then he lists the cost. You end up hating your customer base. You lose autonomy over what you write. You can never pivot to a new interest. You get locked into one identity that bleeds into your whole life.[^9]

Watch what he is actually diagnosing. The interceptor strategy chains you to whatever market you caught. You did not grow those people, so you cannot move them. They came pre-formed with their identity, and your only job was to match it — which means the day your curiosity wanders, your business breaks. The education brand has the opposite shape. Because Koe builds the audience broad and teaches them up, the audience follows *him*, not a fixed topic. When his interest shifts, the nurture sequence shifts, and the people come along because they were learning from him all along.[^10] One playbook owns a market. The other owns the act of teaching, which is portable.

## Implementation Workflow: A Tuesday at the Bottom of the Funnel

It is 6:40 in the morning and you are writing the first post of the day. You do not open with your offer. You open with a problem the reader does not yet know they have — a small ache you name out loud so they feel it for the first time. You hit publish. Nothing is being sold.

Across the week you keep climbing the rungs. Monday's post made them aware the problem exists. Wednesday's shows there is a solution, by sharing a lesson you actually lived. Friday's quietly reveals how much that problem is costing them — their time, their freedom, the years it eats. By the time, weeks later, you mention the product, the reader has been walked up the entire ladder. The sentence "here's what I built" does not feel like an ad. It feels like the obvious last step on a staircase they have been climbing with you the whole time. You did not intercept them at the top. You met them at the bottom and brought them up.[^11]

## The Cultivation Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

- **You resent your audience.** A sure sign you intercepted instead of cultivated — you caught a market you did not choose, and now you are stuck serving people you did not grow.[^12]
- **You cannot pivot without losing everyone.** Your followers came for a fixed topic, not for your teaching, so the moment your curiosity moves, the audience evaporates.[^13]
- **Every post is a pitch.** You are always selling because you never built the climb — there is no education ladder underneath the offer, so the offer has nothing to stand on.
- **You skipped the bottom rungs.** You only ever talk to the already-hot buyer and wonder why your reach is tiny. The broad, unaware bottom of the market is exactly the part you refuse to teach.
- **You niche by demographics, not by the journey.** You picked a customer avatar and froze it, instead of running a sequence that *manufactures* the avatar over time.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The whole model rests on one big claim: that you can reliably educate a broad audience *up* into wanting a specific product, at scale, profitably. Koe presents this as established. It is a [POPULAR SOURCE] assertion from a creator who sells the courses that teach it — a clear case of motivated reasoning, since the strategy and his business are the same thing.[^14] 🚩 No independent evidence is offered for the conversion math.

There is also an unresolved tension inside Koe's own frame. He says identity drives desire and that he creates identities through education.[^15] But he also insists "you are the niche" and that the customer avatar is just your past self.[^16] Those two can pull apart: if you only ever sell to your past self, your audience is bounded by people on your exact path — which is *not* the broad, unsorted bottom of the market he tells you to cultivate. He never resolves whether the created customer is genuinely broad or just a wider slice of people like him.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Koe and the NEPQ corpus are doing the same operation at two different speeds, and the contrast is clarifying. Jeremy Miner's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/self-persuasion-principle-prospect-persuades-themselves|self-persuasion principle]] works inside a single sales conversation: ask the questions that let the prospect talk themselves into the conclusion. Koe takes that and spreads it across an audience and a year. His education sequence is self-persuasion in slow motion — the reader reaches the buying conclusion through months of your free teaching, so that by the time the offer appears it lands as their own idea, not your push. Where they might clash: Miner's method assumes a prospect already in front of you with a felt problem; Koe is manufacturing the felt problem in the first place, upstream, before any conversation exists.

With David Perell there is near-total convergence, but Koe supplies the missing motive. Perell's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/perell-create-not-find-a-niche|create-don't-find a niche]] argues you should invent your category rather than hunt for one. Koe agrees and answers the obvious objection — *why bother, isn't finding easier?* — with the cost list: a found niche traps you, a created one frees you, because the people in it followed your teaching and will follow your pivots. The friction is one of temperament. Perell frames niche-creation as an act of taste and positioning; Koe frames it as an act of conditioning and behavior change, which is the colder, more mechanical reading of the same move.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Plain version: teaching people is a way of changing what they want, and that is the same lever a salesperson pulls in a single conversation — only stretched out over months and aimed at a crowd.

The first handshake is with sales technique, specifically the [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/nepq-eight-stage-engagement-master-spine|NEPQ Eight-Stage Engagement Master Spine]]. In NEPQ, a single human is walked through stages — problem awareness, solution awareness, consequence — inside one phone call, by questions. Customer-creation-through-education is structurally identical but the unit of time and the audience size are blown up enormously. Instead of one prospect across thirty minutes, it is a whole following across a year. The education posts that name the problem are the macro version of a problem-awareness question; the lessons that prove a solution exists are the macro version of solution-awareness; the "this is costing you years" content is the consequence stage. The insight you only get by holding the two together: the difference between a "marketer" and a "salesperson" dissolves. They are running the same compliance ladder; one runs it live and interactive, the other runs it broadcast and asynchronous. A creator's content feed is a sales call that never hangs up, replaying the engagement spine to a new prospect with every scroll. That reframing is dangerous and useful in equal measure — it means an audience is not a community so much as a slow-motion pipeline, and the warmth of "free education" is, structurally, the rapport stage of a sale.

The second handshake is with positioning, through [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/perell-create-not-find-a-niche|Perell — Create, Don't Find a Niche]]. Perell's claim lives in the behavioral-mechanics domain because it is about how you position yourself in a crowded field of attention. Koe's claim lives in business because it is about running an operation — the courses, the cohorts, the content engine. Put them side by side and each fills the other's gap. Perell tells you *what* to do (build the niche) but is light on the mechanism that makes a built niche commercially safe. Koe supplies it: a built niche is safe because its members were educated by you, which means they share your frame and trust your judgment before you ever ask for money. Run the logic the other direction and Koe gains something too — Perell's discipline of specificity protects Koe's strategy from its own failure mode, which is teaching so broadly that you condition no one in particular. The combined claim that neither makes alone: a created customer is the cheapest possible customer to acquire, because the acquisition cost was paid as education the audience experienced as a gift. You did not buy attention with ads or borrow it from sponsors. You earned it by teaching, and the teaching was also the qualifying, the nurturing, and the close, all at once. That is why a 95% margin is plausible — the marketing budget and the product are the same artifact.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication.** If demand can be manufactured upstream by whoever controls the teaching, then "market research" is not neutral discovery — it is surrender. Every hour you spend finding a market is an hour you let someone else educate it first. The aggressive read of Koe is that the most defensible business position is not a better product or a cheaper price but ownership of the audience's *education* — the frame through which they decide what to want. Whoever teaches the market, owns the market.

**Generative Questions.**
- Where does cultivation curdle into manipulation? If education manufactures the desire it later satisfies, is there a line between teaching and grooming a buyer — and who decides where it sits?
- Does this break at scale? Self-persuasion in a sales call works partly because it is intimate; can a broadcast feed actually move a stranger's identity, or only confirm one they already had?
- If everyone adopts customer-creation, does the broad "unaware bottom" get crowded too — and does the advantage just move one rung further upstream?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/every-business-needs-an-education-layer|Every Business Needs an Education Layer]] — the sibling that turns customer-creation into a universal prescription for all businesses, not just creators.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/free-vs-paid-education-convenience-argument|Free vs. Paid Education Convenience Argument]] — the sibling answering why educated customers still pay rather than just self-teach.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/nepq-eight-stage-engagement-master-spine|NEPQ Eight-Stage Engagement Master Spine]] — the same awareness-climbing ladder run live in one conversation instead of broadcast across a year.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/perell-create-not-find-a-niche|Perell — Create, Don't Find a Niche]] — supplies the positioning logic that customer-creation supplies the commercial engine for.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/self-persuasion-principle-prospect-persuades-themselves|Self-Persuasion Principle]] — why an educated customer feels the purchase as their own decision rather than your pitch.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/five-levels-of-awareness-schwartz|Five Levels of Awareness (Schwartz)]] — the rung-by-rung map of the climb the education sequence walks a reader up.
